paragraphs.text: peresat zarathushtrô ahurem mazdãm, ahura mazda mainyô spênishta dâtare gaêthanãm astvaitinãm ashâum kahmâi paoiryô mashyânãm aperese-tûm ýô ahurô mazdå anyô mana ýat zarathushtrâi, kahmâi fradaêsayô daênãm ýãm âhûirîm zarathushtrîm.

i18n.en: Zarathushtra asked Ahura Mazda: 'O Ahura Mazda, most beneficent Spirit, Maker of the material world, righteous one! With whom among mortals, other than me, Zarathushtra, did you first converse, you who are Ahura Mazda? To whom did you teach the Religion, that of Ahura, that of Zarathushtra?'

notes.official:
**The Vendidad's question frame.** Zarathushtra addresses Ahura Mazda with the fixed vocative string the book repeats at every question (vv. 39, 42, 43). *Dātarə gaēθanąm astuuaitinąm* is rendered by the established idiom 'Maker of the material world' (Darmesteter); literally it is 'establisher of the bony (corporeal) living beings': *gaēθā-* is plural ('living beings, settlements') and *astuuant-* is 'possessing bones' (Bartholomae, *AirWb*).

*Ašāum*, vocative of *ašauuan-* 'possessing *aša*' (truth, right order; cognate of Vedic *ṛta-*), is rendered 'righteous one' where Darmesteter has 'thou Holy One'; 'righteous' keeps the link to *aša* visible, and the text applies the same epithet to god and prophet (v. 2). *Anyō mana* is literally 'other than me'; Darmesteter's 'before myself' paraphrases, since 'first' is already carried by *paoiriiō*. The archaic 'thou/didst' of the reference is replaced by the program's modern register throughout (overlay convention).

paragraphs.text: âat mraot ahurô mazdå, ýimâi srîrâi hvãthwâi ashâum zarathushtra ahmâi paoiryô mashyânãm aperese azem ýô ahurô mazdå anyô thwat ýat zarathushtrât, ahmâi fradaêsaêm daênãm ýãm âhûirîm zarathushtrîm.

i18n.en: Then Ahura Mazda said: 'With Yima the fair, of the good herds, O righteous Zarathushtra. With him, first among mortals, other than you, Zarathushtra, did I, who am Ahura Mazda, converse; to him I taught the Religion, that of Ahura, that of Zarathushtra.'

notes.official:
**Yima's epithets.** *Srīra-* 'fair, beautiful' is Yima's standing epithet and is kept as 'fair'. *Huuąθβa-* is a bahuvrīhi 'having good herds'; Darmesteter's 'the good shepherd' follows the Pahlavi commentary he quotes ('he held in good condition herds of men and herds of animals', n. 2), so the WoH text restores the literal 'of the good herds'.

*Yima*, son of *Vīuuaŋhuuaṇt* (Vivanghat), corresponds by name and patronymic to Vedic *Yama*, son of *Vivasvant* (Rigveda 10.14), whom the Veda makes the first mortal to die and the king of the dead; the correspondence is a standard datum of Indo-Iranian philology, and the avesta.org edition of Darmesteter points to Lincoln (*Death, War, and Sacrifice*, 1991, p. 28) for the Yama–Yima comparison. The Avestan Yima is instead the first mortal with whom Ahura Mazda conversed, and a king under whose rule there is no death (v. 5).

paragraphs.text: âat hê mraot zarathushtra azem ýô ahurô mazdå, vîsangha mê ýima srîra vîvanghana meretô beretaca daênayâi, âat mê aêm paityaoxta ýimô srîrô zarathushtra, nôit dâtô ahmi nôit cistô meretô beretaca daênayâi.

i18n.en: Then I said to him, O Zarathushtra, I who am Ahura Mazda: 'Consent, O fair Yima, son of Vivanghat, to be my rememberer and bearer of the Religion.' Then the fair Yima answered me, O Zarathushtra: 'I was not made, I was not taught, to be rememberer and bearer of the Religion.'

notes.official: **Yima declines the Religion.** *Mərətō bərətaca daēnaiiāi* pairs two agent forms built on 'remember, memorize' (*mar-*, cf. Vedic *smṛ-*) and 'carry' (*bar-*): the role is that of an oral tradent who holds the teaching in memory and carries it to others. Darmesteter's 'preacher and bearer' renders the social function; 'rememberer and bearer' restores the lexical core (overlay entry, `inferred`). In Yima's reply, *nōit dātō ahmi* uses the participle of *dā-* 'set, make, establish': 'I was not made' (fashioned or appointed) for this, where Darmesteter has 'I was not born'.

paragraphs.text: âat hê mraom zarathushtra azem ýô ahurô mazdå, ýezi mê ýima nôit vîvîse meretô beretaca daênayâi âat mê gaêthå frâdhaya âat mê gaêthå varedhaya âat mê vîsâi gaêthanãm thrâtâca haretâca aiwyâxshtaca.

i18n.en: Then I said to him, O Zarathushtra, I who am Ahura Mazda: 'If, O Yima, you do not consent to be my rememberer and bearer of the Religion, then make my world increase, then make my world grow; then consent to be the protector, the keeper, and the overseer of my world.'

notes.official: **The alternative office.** *Gaēθā̊* 'my world' is plural in the Avestan ('my living beings, my settlements'); the established singular 'world' is kept in the line. The agent-noun triad is corrected: *θrātar-* is the cognate of Vedic *trātṛ-* 'protector' (Darmesteter: 'nourisher'), *harətar-* is 'keeper, guardian' (Darmesteter: 'ruler'), and *aiβiiāxštar-* is 'overseer'. The WoH text reads 'the protector, the keeper, and the overseer', which describes Yima's office as guardianship of the living rather than provision and rule.

paragraphs.text: âat mê aêm paityaoxta ýimô srîrô zarathushtra, azem tê gaêthå frâdhayeni azem tê gaêthå varedhayeni azem tê vîsâne gaêthanãm thrâtâca haretâca aiwyâxshtaca, nôit mana xshathre bvat aotô vâtô nôit garemô nôit axtish nôit mahrkô.

i18n.en: Then the fair Yima answered me, O Zarathushtra: 'I will make your world increase, I will make your world grow; I will consent to be the protector, the keeper, and the overseer of your world. Under my rule there shall be neither cold wind nor hot, neither disease nor death.'

notes.official: **A reign defined by what is absent.** Yima promises that under his rule (*xšaθra-*, rendered 'rule' throughout; Darmesteter 'while I am king' here and 'sway' elsewhere) there will be 'neither cold wind nor hot, neither disease nor death'. The ideal condition is described by enumerated negation, the figure documented across Sumerian, Hebrew and Greek material in the central entry `paradise-by-negation-no-predation-no-illness-no-aging-cross-corpus` (proposed Avestan extension; see the editor report). Darmesteter's n. 10 records the later tradition (Yašt 9.10) that Yima made immortality reign for a thousand years.

paragraphs.text: âat hê zaya frabarem azem ýô ahurô mazdå suwrãm zaranaênîm ashtrãmca zaranyô- paêsîm.

i18n.en: Then I, who am Ahura Mazda, brought him two implements: a golden suwra and a goad inlaid with gold.

notes.official:
**The two implements are lexically uncertain.** Ahura Mazda gives Yima two *zaiia* 'implements': a *suβrā* 'golden' and an *aštrā* 'gold-adorned' (*zaraniiō.paēsī-*).

*Aštrā-* is secure: the Vendidad uses it in its penal formulas for the instrument of the prescribed strokes (*aspahe aštrā*, 'the horse's goad/whip'), and it is cognate with Vedic *aṣṭrā-* 'goad'. Darmesteter's 'poniard' follows later Persian investiture imagery (his n. 4: 'the sword and the seal, the ring and the crown', Firdausi). The WoH text reads 'goad'.

*Suβrā-* has no secure etymology or parallel. 'Seal' or 'ring' is the Pahlavi tradition (Darmesteter even alternates 'seal' at v. 30 and 'ring' at v. 38); other objects have also been proposed. Because no rendering is secure, the word is transliterated as **suwra** in every occurrence (vv. 6, 10, 14, 18, 30, 38), and this note is the place where the options are recorded (overlay entry, `inferred`).

**Numbering.** Darmesteter (n. 3) treats v. 6 as commentator's quotations and appends 'Behold, here Yima bears the royal sway!' to it; in Geldner that clause is v. 7 (see there).

paragraphs.text: ýimô asti berethe xshathrayå.

i18n.en: Yima is to bear the kingly rule.

notes.official: **Geldner's v. 7.** *Yimō asti bərəθe xšaθraiiā̊*: a short nominal clause in which *bərəθe* is a dative infinitive 'to bear'. The WoH text renders it as a statement of office, 'Yima is to bear the kingly rule'. Darmesteter relocates the clause to the end of his v. 6 as an exclamation ('Behold, here Yima bears the royal sway!') and prints his v. 7 as '[Obscure.]'; Geldner's numbering is followed here (overlay convention). The clause is abrupt in context and its function in the narrative remains unclear.

paragraphs.text: âat ýimâi xshathrâi thrisatô-zima hañjaseñti, âat hê îm zå bvat perene pasvãmca staoranãmca mashyânãmca sûnãmca vayãmca âthrãmca suxrãm saociñtãm nôit hîm gâtvô viñden pasvasca staorâca mashyâca.

i18n.en: Then three hundred winters of Yima's rule were completed, and this earth of his became full of flocks and herds and men and dogs and birds and red blazing fires; and the flocks and herds and men found no room on it.

notes.official:
**Reckoning by winters.** The reign is counted in *zim-* 'winters' (*θrisatō.zima-* 'of three hundred winters'), and the unit is kept because the coming catastrophe is itself a winter (v. 22): count and threat share one word. *Haṇjasəṇti* 'come together' is rendered 'were completed' (Darmesteter: 'passed away').

*Pasu-* and *staora-* are the Avestan pair for small and large livestock, rendered 'flocks and herds' at every occurrence; Darmesteter switches to 'sheep and oxen' for the same words at vv. 25 and 33. The catalogue that follows (flocks, herds, men, dogs, birds, 'red blazing fires') counts fire among the kinds that multiply and must be housed, and the same catalogue returns as the inventory of the Vara (v. 25).

paragraphs.text: âat ýimâi paiti-vaêdhaêm, ýima srîra vîvanghana perene îm zå hañgata pasvãmca staoranãmca mashyânãmca sûnãmca vayãmca âthrãmca suxrãm saociñtãm nôit hîm gâtvô viñdeñti pasvasca staorâca mashyâca.

i18n.en: Then I warned Yima: 'O fair Yima, son of Vivanghat, this earth is full, crowded with flocks and herds and men and dogs and birds and red blazing fires; the flocks and herds and men find no room.'

paragraphs.text: âat ýimô frashûsat raocå â upa rapithwãm hû paiti adhwanem, hô imãm zãm aiwishvat suwrya zaranaênya avi dim sifat ashtraya uityaojanô, fritha speñta ârmaite fraca shva vîca nemangha barethre pasvãmca staoranãmca mashyânãmca.

i18n.en: Then Yima went forth toward the lights, southward, on the path of the sun. He pressed this earth with the golden suwra and pierced it with the goad, saying: 'O dear Spenta Armaiti, move forward and spread apart, in reverence, to bear flocks and herds and men.'

notes.official:
**The enlargement rite.** *Raocā̊ ā* is accusative plural with the directional particle: 'toward the lights', not Darmesteter's 'in light', which follows the later image of Yima himself shining (his n. 5). *Rapiθβā-* is 'midday'; in Iranian orientation the midday quarter is the south, hence 'southward' (Darmesteter n. 6: the south as the region of paradise, the north as the seat of cold and the demons).

Spenta Armaiti is the being associated with the earth (Darmesteter: 'the Genius of the Earth'). *Friθa-* 'dear' (cognate of Vedic *priya-*) is Darmesteter's 'kindly'; *nəmaŋha* 'with homage, in reverence', which he leaves unrendered, is kept. The verbs of handling, *aiwišuuat* ('pressed') and *sifat* ('pierced'; Darmesteter 'bored'), are uncertain and follow the reference construal; on the implements see v. 6.

paragraphs.text: âat ýimô imãm zãm vîshâvayat aêva thrishva ahmât masyehîm ýatha para ahmât as, tem ithra fracareñta pasvasca staorâca mashyâca hvãm anu ushtîm zaoshemca ýatha kathaca hê zaoshô.

i18n.en: Then Yima made this earth expand by one third beyond what it had been before; and flocks and herds and men went forth upon it, according to their own wish and pleasure, in whatever way it pleased him.

notes.official: **One third larger.** *Θrišuua-* is 'a third part' (not *karšuuar-*, the regional 'clime', which does not occur in this chapter). In *yaθa kaθaca hē zaošō* the enclitic *hē* is singular, so 'in whatever way it pleased him' keeps the grammar while leaving the referent (Yima, or each creature) as open as the Avestan; Darmesteter's 'as many as he wished' adds a quantity the clause does not state.

notes.official: **Abbreviated formula, restored.** Geldner prints vv. 12-14 as one unit: *pərəne ... mašiiānąmca*. The ellipsis stands for the rest of the v. 8 formula, the whole v. 9 warning and the whole v. 10 rite, and the printed final word *mašiiānąmca* is the last word of v. 10 ('and men'). Following the overlay ellipsis convention, the omitted text is restored verbatim from vv. 8-10 inside square brackets, with '(v. 13:)' and '(v. 14:)' marking where Geldner's verse divisions fall. Only the words outside the brackets are printed in the source at this point; everything inside them is attested in full earlier in the chapter.

paragraphs.text: âat ýimô imãm zãm vîshâvayat dva thrishva ahmât masyehîm ýatha para ahmât as, tem ithra fracareñta pasvasca staorâca mashyâca hvãm anu ushtîm zaoshemca ýatha kathaca hê zaoshô.

i18n.en: Then Yima made this earth expand by two thirds beyond what it had been before; and flocks and herds and men went forth upon it, according to their own wish and pleasure, in whatever way it pleased him.

paragraphs.text: âat ýimâi xshathrâi nava-satô-zima hañjaseñti, âat hê îm zå bvat perene pasvãmca staoranãmca mashyânãmca sûnãmca vayãmca âthrãmca suxrãm saociñtãm, nôit hîm gâtvô viñden pasvasca staorâca mashyâca.

i18n.en: Then nine hundred winters of Yima's rule were completed, and this earth of his became full of flocks and herds and men and dogs and birds and red blazing fires; and the flocks and herds and men found no room on it.

paragraphs.text: âat ýimâi paiti-vaêdhaêm, ýima srîra vîvanghana perene îm zå hañgata pasvãmca staoranãmca mashyânãmca sûnãmca vayãmca âthrãmca suxrãm saociñtãm, nôit hîm gâtvô viñdeñti pasvasca staorâca mashyâca.

i18n.en: Then I warned Yima: 'O fair Yima, son of Vivanghat, this earth is full, crowded with flocks and herds and men and dogs and birds and red blazing fires; the flocks and herds and men find no room.'

paragraphs.text: âat ýimô frashûsat raocå â upa rapithwãm hû paiti adhwanem, hô imãm zãm aiwishvat suwrya zaranaênya avi dim sifat ashtraya uityaojanô, fritha speñta ârmaite fraca shva vîca nemangha barethre pasvãmca staoranãmca mashyânãmca.

i18n.en: Then Yima went forth toward the lights, southward, on the path of the sun. He pressed this earth with the golden suwra and pierced it with the goad, saying: 'O dear Spenta Armaiti, move forward and spread apart, in reverence, to bear flocks and herds and men.'

paragraphs.text: âat ýimô imãm zãm vîshâvayat thribyô thrishvaêibyô ahmât masyehîm ýatha para ahmât as, tem ithra fracareñta pasvasca staorâca mashyâca hvãm anu ushtîm zaoshemca ýatha kathaca hê zaoshô!

i18n.en: Then Yima made this earth expand by three thirds beyond what it had been before; and flocks and herds and men went forth upon it, according to their own wish and pleasure, in whatever way it pleased him.

notes.official: **Three thirds, not two.** The third enlargement is *θribiiō θrišuuaēibiiō* 'by three thirds', completing the series one / two / three thirds (vv. 11, 15, 19). Darmesteter prints 'two-thirds' here, repeating v. 15; that is an error in the reference, and the WoH text follows the Avestan.

paragraphs.text: hañjamanem frabarata ýô dadhvå ahurô mazdå hathra mainyaoibyô ýazataêibyô srûtô airyene vaêjahi vanghuyå dâityayå, hañjamanem frabarata ýô ýimô xshaêtô hvãthwô hathra vahishtaêibyô mashyâkaêibyô srûtô airyene vaêjahi vanghuyå dâityayå.

i18n.en: He who is the Maker, Ahura Mazda, convened an assembly with the spiritual Yazatas — he, renowned in Airyana Vaejah of the Good Daitya. He who is Yima the radiant, of the good herds, convened an assembly with the best of mortals — he, renowned in Airyana Vaejah of the Good Daitya.

notes.official:
**Two assemblies.** Ahura Mazda convenes (*frabarata*, 'brought forth') an assembly (*haṇjamana-*) with the *mainiiauua* Yazatas, and Yima one with 'the best of mortals'. *Mainiiauua-*, the adjective of *mainiiu-* 'spirit', means 'spiritual, belonging to the mental existence' and contrasts with *gaēθiia-* 'material'; Darmesteter's 'celestial' adds a spatial image. The Yazatas ('beings worthy of worship') are left untranslated, as is standard.

*Srūtō* is nominative singular masculine and cannot agree with the locative *airiiene vaējahi*; it describes the subject: 'he, renowned in Airyana Vaejah'. Darmesteter attaches it to the place ('of high renown'). *Vaŋhuiiā̊ dāitiiaiiā̊* is genitive, 'of the Good Daitya' (the river of Airyana Vaejah, Vd 1.2), not 'by the Vanguhi Daitya'. Yima's epithet here is *xšaēta-* 'radiant', distinct from *srīra-* 'fair'; Darmesteter renders both as 'fair'. *Yima xšaēta* is the source of the later name Jamšēd.

paragraphs.text: â-tat hañjamanem paiti-jasat ýô dadhvå ahurô mazdå hathra mainyaoibyô ýazataêibyô srûtô airyene vaêjahi vanghuyå dâityayå, â-tat hañjamanem paiti-jasât ýô ýimô xshaêtô hvãthwô hathra vahishtaêibyô mashyâkaêibyô srûtô airyene vaêjahi vanghuyå dâityayå.

i18n.en: To that assembly came he who is the Maker, Ahura Mazda, with the spiritual Yazatas — he, renowned in Airyana Vaejah of the Good Daitya. To that assembly came he who is Yima the radiant, of the good herds, with the best of mortals — he, renowned in Airyana Vaejah of the Good Daitya.

paragraphs.text: âat aoxta ahurô mazdå ýimâi, ýima srîra vîvanghana avi ahûm astvañtem akhem zimô jangheñtu ýahmat haca staxrô mrûrô zyå, avi ahûm astvañtem akhem zimô jangheñtu ýahmat haca paurvô snaodhô vafra snaêzhât barezishtaêibyô gairibyô bãshnubyô areduyå.

i18n.en: Then Ahura Mazda said to Yima: 'O fair Yima, son of Vivanghat! Upon the material world the evil winters shall come, from which comes fierce, deadly frost; upon the material world the evil winters shall come, from which the cloud shall first snow down snowflakes on the highest mountains, on the heights, an aredvi deep.

notes.official:
**The evil winters.** *Aγəm zimō* is ambiguous between 'evil winter(s)' and 'the evil of winter' (*zimō* may be genitive singular); the plural verb *jaŋhəṇtu* supports the standard 'the evil winters', and the alternative is recorded here. The Pahlavi commentary names these winters *malkōsān*, after a demon *Mahrkūša* 'death-causing' (Darmesteter n. 13); that name does not occur in the Avestan text and is not introduced into the English. *Arəδuiiā̊* is rendered as a measure of depth ('an aredvi deep'), following Darmesteter and the commentary's gloss (n. 14: 'one Vitasti two fingers'), though it may instead be the name Arədvī.

**Comparative note.** A warning to one chosen individual of a coming catastrophe that will destroy the living, followed by the command to build a refuge (v. 25), is the structural core that Darmesteter, in his introduction to this Fargard, compared with the biblical and Mesopotamian flood narratives. The catastrophe here is winter, frost and snow, with a meltwater flood only as its aftermath (v. 24), and the story has also been read as an indigenous Iranian myth of a catastrophic winter rather than an adaptation of the flood tradition (the question is discussed in Boyce, *A History of Zoroastrianism* I, 1975, pp. 92 ff.). See the proposed central entry `vara-tevah-eleppu-divinely-instructed-refuge-against-world-catastrophe-cross-corpus` (`inferred`).

paragraphs.text: thrizhatca idha ýima gêush apa-jasat ýatca anghat thwyãstemaêshu asanghãm ýatca anghat bareshnush paiti gairinãm ýatca jãfnushva raonãm paxrumaêshu nmânaêshu.

i18n.en: And a third of the cattle, O Yima, shall go away from here: those that are in the most dreadful of places, and those on the heights of the mountains, and those in the depths of the river valleys, in sheltered dwellings.

notes.official: **A third of the cattle.** The verse opens with *θrižat-* 'a third', which Darmesteter does not translate ('And the beasts that live in the wilderness ... shall take shelter in underground abodes'). *Apa-gam-* is 'go away, get away'; whether this third escapes the winter or perishes is not decided by the verb, and 'shall go away from here' keeps that open. Darmesteter's 'underground abodes' reflects the later belief that the Vara was subterranean (his n. 30); *paxruma-* is of uncertain meaning, and 'sheltered dwellings' is the neutral rendering. *Raona-* is 'river', hence 'river valleys'. The construal of the whole verse remains disputed (overlay entry, `inferred`).

paragraphs.text: parô zimô aêtanghå danghush anghat beretô vâstrem tem âfsh paurva vazaidhyâi pasca vîtaxti vafrahe abdaca idha ýima anguhe astvaite sadayât ýat idha pasêush anumayehe padhem vaênâite.

i18n.en: Before the winter, this land would bear pasture, before the waters are to flood it after the melting of the snow; and it will seem a wonder, O Yima, in the material world, if the footprint of a sheep is seen here.

notes.official: **Before the meltwater.** The verse is syntactically obscure. The WoH text follows Darmesteter's construal but takes *pauruua* as 'before, first' (the adjective *pauruua-* 'former'), not 'abundantly' (which would require *pouru-* 'much'). The resulting order (pasture before the winter, then the waters flooding the land after the snow melts) is the order that *pasca vītaxti vafrahe* 'after the melting of the snow' requires. A sheep's footprint becomes a wonder: the land is emptied of livestock.

paragraphs.text: âat tem varem kerenava caretu-drâjô kemcit paiti cathrushanãm hathra taoxma upa-bara pasvãmca staoranãmca mashyânãmca sûnãmca vayãmca âthrãmca suxrãm saociñtãm, âat tem varem kerenava caretu-drâjô kemcit paiti cathrushanãm narãm aiwi-xshôithne caretu-drâjô kemcit paiti cathrushanãm gavãm gâvayanem.

i18n.en: Then make the Vara, the length of a race-course on each of its four sides; bring there the seeds of flocks and herds and men and dogs and birds and red blazing fires. Then make the Vara, the length of a race-course on each of its four sides, as a dwelling for men; the length of a race-course on each of its four sides, as a fold for cattle.

notes.official:
**The Vara.** *Vara-*, from *var-* 'to cover, enclose', means an enclosure; the word is transliterated, as in all scholarship (Middle Persian *war*, 'the Var of Jam'), because it names a unique structure. Its plan is given by a measure: *carətu.drājah-* 'having the length of a race-course' *kəmcit paiti caθrušanąm* 'on each of the four sides'. The text describes a square without using the word 'square' (Darmesteter: 'on every side of the square'). The Pahlavi commentary gives two *hāθra* per side, and Darmesteter estimates a *hāθra* at about an English mile (n. 18).

Yima is to bring *taoxma* 'seeds' of every kind in the v. 8 catalogue, including the fires. *Taoxman-* 'seed, stock' is rendered 'seeds' uniformly. The preservation of the seed of humankind and of animals through a world-ending catastrophe is a recurring element of the Mesopotamian and Hebrew flood traditions: the Sumerian Flood Story's 'seed of humankind', Gilgamesh XI's 'seed of all living creatures' loaded into the boat (XI 27, 82-85), and Genesis 6:19-20. See the central entry `preservation-of-the-seed-of-humankind-and-animals-flood-aitia-cross-corpus` (proposed Avestan extension).

**Wheel of Heaven reading (interpretive; not part of the translation).** The project reads the Vara, alongside Noah's *tevah* and Atra-ḫasīs's boat, as a deliberately designed preservation of living stock carried out on instruction from a superior authority (in the text, Ahura Mazda). This synthesis is recorded as the proposed central entry `vara-as-designed-preservation-habitat-woh-reading` (`speculative`, ratified at human sign-off). It does not shape the English, which renders the Avestan as any Iranist would.

paragraphs.text: hathra âpem frâtat-caya hâthrô-masanghem adhwanem hathra marekhå avastaya, avi mat zairi-gaonem mat hvairyeite ajyamnem, hathra nmânå avastaya katemca fraskembemca fravâremca pairi-vâremca.

i18n.en: There make the waters flow along a course a hathra in length; there settle birds, by the golden-green, by the food that is eaten and never fails. There establish dwellings: a chamber and a pillared porch and a front enclosure and a surrounding enclosure.

notes.official:
**Water, birds, dwellings.** Darmesteter's 'on the green that never fades' attaches 'never' to the colour, but *ajiiamna-* 'unfailing' qualifies the food that is eaten (*x'airiieite*), and *zairi.gaona-* is simply 'golden-green coloured'. The WoH text restores both: 'by the golden-green, by the food that is eaten and never fails'.

The four dwelling terms are rare; Darmesteter notes that the last three are hapax legomena of doubtful meaning (n. 20) and offers 'house, balcony, courtyard, gallery'. The WoH renderings follow the roots instead: *kata-* 'chamber, storeroom'; *fraskəmba-*, containing *skəmba-* 'pillar' (Vedic *skambha-*), 'pillared porch'; *frauuāra-* and *pairiuuāra-*, built on *var-* 'enclose' with *fra-* 'in front' and *pairi-* 'around', 'front enclosure' and 'surrounding enclosure' (overlay entry, `inferred`).

paragraphs.text: hathra vîspanãm narãm nâirinãmca taoxma upa-bara ýôi heñti ainghå zemô mazishtaca vahishtaca sraêshtaca, hathra vîspanãm gêush saredhanãm taoxma upa-bara ýôi heñti ainghå zemô mazishtaca vahishtaca sraêshtaca.

i18n.en: There bring the seeds of all men and women who are, on this earth, the greatest and best and fairest; there bring the seeds of all kinds of cattle that are, on this earth, the greatest and best and fairest.

notes.official: **Selection by excellence.** The seeds are of the 'greatest, best and fairest' (*mazišta-, vahišta-, sraēšta-*) of men, women and cattle. *Sraēšta-* is the superlative of Yima's own epithet *srīra-* 'fair', so it is rendered 'fairest' at every occurrence (vv. 27, 35, 41); Darmesteter's 'finest' here and 'happiest' at v. 41 hide the link. As a comparative observation, the principle of selection differs from Genesis, where the survivors are Noah's household and pairs of every kind (Gen 6:18-20; 7:2-3); here the criterion is excellence of stock, made explicit again by the exclusions of v. 29.

paragraphs.text: hathra vîspanãm urvaranãm taoxma upa-bara ýôi heñti ainghå zemô barezishtaca hubaoidhitemaca, hathra vîspanãm hvarethanãm taoxma upa-bara ýôi heñti ainghå zemô hvarezishtaca hubaoidhitemaca, tê kerenava mithwaire ajyamnem vîspem â ahmât ýat aête narô varefshva anghen.

i18n.en: There bring the seeds of all plants that are, on this earth, the tallest and most fragrant; there bring the seeds of all foods that are, on this earth, the most delicious and most fragrant. Make them in pairs, to be inexhaustible, all of them, for as long as those men shall be in the Varas.

notes.official:
**Plants, foods, pairs.** *Uruuarā-* is the general word for 'plant' and *x'arəθa-* is 'food, what is eaten'. Darmesteter's 'trees' and 'fruits' follow the Pahlavi commentary's examples (cypress and plane; date and citron, nn. 22-23), which narrow the categories. *Miθβairē* is 'in pairs'. Darmesteter's 'two of every kind' echoes the King James wording of Gen 6:19, and the WoH text avoids that echo so that any comparison is made in commentary, not in the English.

*Varəfšuua* 'in the Varas' is a locative plural, with a plural demonstrative at vv. 39, 41, 42; Darmesteter flattens it to 'the Vara'. The plural is kept. It may refer to the Vara's three parts (v. 30) or be a plural of extent.

paragraphs.text: mâ athra frakavô mâ apakavô mâ apâvayô mâ haredhish mâ driwish mâ daiwish mâ kasvîsh mâ vîzbârish mâ vîmîtô-dañtânô mâ paêsô ýô vîteretô-tanush mâdha-cim anyãm daxshtanãm ýôi heñti angrahe mainyêush daxshtem mashyâishca paiti nidhâtem.

i18n.en: Let there be there no one humped in front, no one humped behind, no impotent(?) one, no lunatic(?), no malicious(?) one, no liar(?), no spiteful(?) one, no jealous(?) one, no one with misshapen teeth, no leper whose body is set apart, nor any other of the marks that are the mark of Angra Mainyu, laid upon mortals.

notes.official:
**The exclusion list (partly unresolved; escalated).** The text bars from the Vara a series of conditions it calls the 'marks' (*daxšta-*) of Angra Mainyu laid upon mortals. Where the morphology is transparent, the WoH text follows it. *Frakauua-* and *apakauua-* are 'humped in front' and 'humped behind' (*fra-* 'forward', *apa-* 'back'), against Darmesteter's 'humpbacked, bulged forward'. *Vīmitō.dantan-* is 'with mis-measured (misshapen) teeth', not 'decayed'. *Paēsa- yō vītərətō.tanuš* is 'a leper whose body is set apart' (Darmesteter n. 24 cites Herodotus 1.139 on lepers being kept out of towns).

The six middle items (*apāuuaiia-, hərəδi-, driβi-, daiβi-, kasuuī-, vīzbāri-*) are of uncertain meaning. Scholars divide between moral faults (Darmesteter's 'impotent, lunatic, malicious, liar, spiteful, jealous') and bodily defects. Darmesteter's renderings are kept as the reference default, and the question is escalated for human ruling. Darmesteter's n. 25 reads the list as making the new humanity 'exempt from all moral and physical deformities'.

paragraphs.text: fratemem dainghêush nava perethwô kerenava madhemô xshvash nitemô tishrô, fratemem perethwô hazangrem narãm nâirinãmca taoxma upa-bara madhemô xshvash sata nitemô tishrô sata, aiwica tê varefshva suwrya zaranaênya apica tem varem mareza dvarem raocanem hvâraoxshnem añtare-naêmât.

i18n.en: In the foremost part of the place make nine passages, in the middle part six, in the lowest three. To the passages of the foremost part bring a thousand seeds of men and women, of the middle part six hundred, of the lowest three hundred. And ⟨stroke⟩ over the Varas with the golden suwra, and seal up that Vara: a door, a window self-shining from within.'

notes.official:
**Plan and sealing of the Vara.** *Fratəma-, maδəma-, nitəma-* are 'foremost, middle, lowest'; Darmesteter's 'largest ... smallest' infers size from the numbers. *Pərətu-* is a passage or crossing (Middle Persian *puhl* 'bridge'), so 'passages', not 'streets'. The seeds of men and women are distributed 1,000 / 600 / 300; Darmesteter (n. 26) suggests the three parts answer to the three social classes.

**The sealing clause.** *Aiβica tē varəfšuua suβriia zaranaēniia* has no verb. Its preverb *aiβi-* is read with the verb *marəz-* of the next clause (*aiβi-marəz-* 'stroke over'; *api-marəz-* 'smear over, seal up'). The WoH text therefore supplies ⟨stroke⟩ in angle brackets, the overlay sign for editorial supply; importing *aiwišuuat* 'pressed' from v. 10 would add a verb the clause does not imply, and Darmesteter merges both clauses into 'That Vara thou shalt seal up with thy golden seal'. The closing 'a door, a window self-shining from within' (*duuarəm raocanəm x'āraoxšnəm aṇtarə.naēmāt*) is likewise verbless and is left as an apposition, where Darmesteter supplies 'thou shalt make'.

A sealed refuge with a single light-opening can be compared with the boat-window of the flood narratives (Gen 6:16; 8:6; Gilgamesh XI); see `vara-tevah-eleppu-divinely-instructed-refuge-against-world-catastrophe-cross-corpus`. Unlike the boat-window, which is opened after the storm, the Vara's window is built in and is described as shining by itself.

paragraphs.text: âat mãsta ýimô, kutha tê azem varem kerenavâne ýâ mê aoxta ahurô mazdå, âat aoxta ahurô mazdå ýimâi, ýima srîra vîvanghana ainghå zemô pâshnâbya vîspara zastaêibya vîxadha mãnayen ahe ýatha nû mashyâka xshivisti zemê vîshâvayeiñte.

i18n.en: Then Yima thought: 'How shall I make the Vara of which Ahura Mazda has spoken to me?' Then Ahura Mazda said to Yima: 'O fair Yima, son of Vivanghat, tread this earth apart with your heels, knead it apart with your hands, in the way that men now spread out soft earth.'

notes.official: **Tread and knead.** Ahura Mazda's instruction compares the work to the way 'men now spread out soft earth' (*xšuuisti zəmē vīšāuuaiieiṇte*). Darmesteter's 'as the potter does when kneading the potter's clay' is an interpretive expansion: no potter and no clay are named. The verb *vīšāuuaiia-* 'spread out' is the same verb used for Yima's enlargements of the earth (vv. 11, 15, 19), and the WoH text keeps the image of spreading. Darmesteter's n. 27 notes the Shahnameh tradition of Jamshid teaching the demons to knead clay and build.

paragraphs.text: âat ýimô avatha kerenaot ýatha dim ishat ahurô mazdå ainghå zemô pâshnâbya vîsparat zastaêibya vîxadhat mãnayen ahe ýatha nû mashyâka xshivisti zemê vîshâvayeiñte.

i18n.en: Then Yima did so, as Ahura Mazda wished of him: he trod this earth apart with his heels, he kneaded it apart with his hands, in the way that men now spread out soft earth.

notes.official: **Part of the text.** Darmesteter prints this verse in brackets as supplied 'From the Vendidad Sada' (n. 28); Geldner prints it in the text, and it is translated here without brackets (overlay numbering convention). It repeats v. 31's instruction as executed.

paragraphs.text: nôit athra frakavô nôit apakavô nôit apâvayô nôit haredhish nôit driwish nôit daiwish nôit kasvîsh nôit vîzbârish nôit vîmîtô-dañtânô nôit paêsô ýô vîteretô-tanush naêdha-cim anyãm daxshtanãm ýôi heñti angrahe mainyêush daxshtem mashyâishca paiti nidhâtem.

i18n.en: There was there no one humped in front, no one humped behind, no impotent(?) one, no lunatic(?), no malicious(?) one, no liar(?), no spiteful(?) one, no jealous(?) one, no one with misshapen teeth, no leper whose body is set apart, nor any other of the marks that are the mark of Angra Mainyu, laid upon mortals.

paragraphs.text: fratemem dainghêush nava perethwô kerenaot madhemô xshvash nitemô tishrô fratemem perethwô hazangrem narãm nâirinãmca taoxma upa-barat madhemô xshvash sata nitemô tishrô sata, aiwica hô varefshva suwrya zaranaênya apica hô varem marezat dvarem raocanem hvâraoxshnem añtare-naêmât.

i18n.en: In the foremost part of the place he made nine passages, in the middle part six, in the lowest three. To the passages of the foremost part he brought a thousand seeds of men and women, of the middle part six hundred, of the lowest three hundred. And he ⟨stroked⟩ over the Varas with the golden suwra, and he sealed up that Vara: a door, a window self-shining from within.

notes.official: **Execution of v. 30.** The supplied verb is again marked ⟨stroked⟩ (see v. 30). Darmesteter renders the same *suβrā* as 'the golden ring' here after 'thy golden seal' at v. 30, which shows how unsettled the identification of the object is; the WoH text keeps the transliteration 'suwra' (see v. 6).

paragraphs.text: dâtare gaêthanãm astvaitinãm ashâum cayô âat aête raocå anghen ashâum ahura mazda ýô avatha â-raocayeite aêtaêshva varefshva ýô ýimô kerenaot.

i18n.en: O Maker of the material world, righteous one! What, then, are those lights, O righteous Ahura Mazda, that shine there in those Varas which Yima made?

paragraphs.text: âat aoxta ahurô mazdå, hvadhâtaca raocå stidhâtaca, hakeret zî irixtahe sadhayaca vaênaite starasca måsca hvareca.

i18n.en: Then Ahura Mazda said: 'Self-created lights and lights created in the world. For only once is the setting and rising of the stars and the moon and the sun seen.

notes.official:
**Self-created lights.** *X'aδāta-* is a transparent compound of *x'a-* 'self' and *dāta-* 'created': 'self-created', not Darmesteter's 'uncreated'. *Stiδāta-* pairs *dāta-* with *stī-* 'existence': lights created in the (material) world. The phrase *anaγra raocā̊* 'endless lights', which lies behind Darmesteter's gloss 'The endless light, which is eternal' (n. 29), does not occur in this verse. Darmesteter glosses the second class as 'artificial lights'; that gloss is reception history and is not adopted in the line.

*Hakərət* is the cognate of Vedic *sakṛt* 'once', and Darmesteter's 'The one thing missed there is the sight of the stars, the moon, and the sun' does not render it. With *irixta-* 'setting' (from *ric-* 'leave') and *saδaiia-* 'appearing, rising', the WoH text reads: 'For only once is the setting and rising of the stars and the moon and the sun seen'. This coheres with v. 41's 'they consider to be a day what is a year'. Darmesteter's n. 30 explains the absence of the heavenly lights by placing the Vara underground; the Avestan does not say so. Darmesteter also closes his v. 40 with 'and a year seems only as a day', which in Geldner opens v. 41.

paragraphs.text: taêca ayare mainyeñte ýat ýâre, cathwaresatem aiwi-gâmanãm dvaêibya haca nerebya dva nara us-zayeiñte mithwana strica nairyasca atha aêtaêshãm ýôi gêush saredhanãm, taêca narô sraêshta gaya jvaiñti aêtaêshva varefshva ýô ýimô kerenaot.

i18n.en: And they consider to be a day what is a year. Every forty years, from two human beings two human beings are born, a pair, female and male; and so too for those of the kinds of cattle. And these men live the fairest life in those Varas which Yima made.'

notes.official: **Life in the Vara.** *Caθβarəsatəm aiβi.gāmanąm* 'every forty years': *aiβi.gāma-* ('the on-coming', i.e. winter) is a different word from *zim-* 'winter' (vv. 8, 22) and is the ordinary reckoning of years, so it is rendered 'years'. The dual phrasing 'from two human beings two human beings are born, a pair, female and male' is kept because it states a replacement rate that Darmesteter's 'to every couple two are born' paraphrases away; the order 'female and male' follows *strīca nairiiasca*, which Darmesteter reverses. *Sraēšta- gaiia-* is 'the fairest life' (Darmesteter 'happiest'; see v. 27). The opening clause belongs to v. 41 in Geldner (see v. 40).

paragraphs.text: dâtare gaêthanãm astvaitinãm ashâum, kô avatha daênãm mâzdayasnîm vî-barat aêtaêshva varefshva ýô ýimô kerenaot, âat aoxta ahurô mazdå, vîsh karshipta spitama zarathushtra.

i18n.en: O Maker of the material world, righteous one! Who spread the Mazda-worshipping Religion in those Varas which Yima made? Then Ahura Mazda said: 'The bird Karshipta, O Spitama Zarathushtra.'

notes.official: **The bird Karshipta.** *Vī.barat*, with the preverb *vī-* 'apart, abroad', is 'spread', not Darmesteter's 'brought'. *Māzdaiiasnī-* is 'Mazda-worshipping'; Darmesteter's 'the Religion of Mazda' moves the attribute from the worshippers to the god. In the later Pahlavi tradition (Bundahišn, quoted in Darmesteter n. 34) Karšift dwells in the heavens and recites the Avesta in the language of birds. The vocative *spitama zaraθuštra* is kept; Darmesteter prints 'holy Zarathushtra'.

paragraphs.text: dâtare ... ashâum, kô aêshãm asti anghuca ratushca, âat mraot ahurô mazdå, urvatat-narô zarathushtra tûmca ýô zarathushtrô! ashem vohû...!!

i18n.en: O Maker [of the material world], righteous one! Who is their lord and master? Then Ahura Mazda said: 'Urvatat-nara, O Zarathushtra, and you, who are Zarathushtra.' Ashem vohu …

notes.official:
**Lord and master.** *Aŋhuca ratušca* is the fixed Avestan pair of authorities, *ahu-* and *ratu-*, best known from the Ahuna Vairya prayer (*yaθā ahū vairiiō aθā ratuš*). 'Lord and master' is the standard English for the pair. The line names two figures but does not assign the roles; the later tradition reported by Darmesteter (n. 35) makes Urvatat-nara, Zarathushtra's son, the temporal *ahu* and Zarathushtra the spiritual *ratu*.

**Apparatus.** The opening vocative is abbreviated in the source (*dātarə ... ašāum*) and is restored from v. 1 in square brackets. The closing *ašəm vohū ...* is the incipit of the Ashem Vohu prayer, abbreviated as a liturgical rubric. The prayer does not occur in full in this chapter, so under the overlay convention it is left as a transliterated incipit with the source's ellipsis ('Ashem vohu …').
